title: Disjoint spectral sets and Rosenblum theory
subtitle: G2 lecture 067000 · baseline companion · needs expansion
adaptation: First-pass source-derived outline. Section excerpts and any vector equation come from the spoken lecture and its display-only mathematics appendix. Expand with worked mathematics, proofs and topic-specific diagrams.

slides.title: The problem and its setting
slides.lead: For self-adjoint Sylvester coefficients, an ordered real spectral gap produces an integral of decaying semigroups.
body: Without self-adjointness there is no such spectral order. A complex contour of resolvents provides a different construction that requires only disjoint spectra of bounded operators. The central question is whether the spectra of two bounded operators are disjoint. For bounded complex operators on Banach spaces, this is enough for the Sylvester operator to have a bounded inverse. The method is associated with Rosenblum, and its engine is a contour integral of resolvents.

slides.title: Recall the resolvent
slides.lead: Let A be a bounded operator.
body: For a complex number z outside its spectrum, the operator z times the identity minus A has a bounded inverse. We call that inverse the resolvent of A at z. The resolvent is a function of z. It is analytic away from the spectrum, and integrating it around a closed contour can select spectral components of the operator. For a one-by-one matrix consisting of scalar a, the resolvent is just one over z minus a. Its integral around a positively oriented circle is two pi i if the circle encloses a and zero otherwise, after dividing by the usual normalization. Thus contour integration can detect whether a spectral value lies inside a curve.

slides.title: The two-resolvent integrand
slides.lead: Let A act on a Banach space Y and B act on another Banach space X.
body: Our right-hand side C maps X to Y. For a complex number z outside both spectra, form the resolvent of A at z, followed by C, followed by the resolvent of B at z. Call this operator K of z. Notice the order. The right resolvent acts first on a vector in X, C sends that vector into Y, and the left resolvent then acts on Y. Every composition is type-correct even though the two Banach spaces need not be the same. The proposed solution is the contour integral of K, divided by two pi i, over a positively oriented closed contour that encloses all of A's spectrum and none of B's spectrum.

slides.title: The cancellation identity
slides.lead: Write R A for the resolvent of A and R B for the resolvent of B, evaluated at the same z.
body: Because z identity minus A multiplied by R A is the identity, we can rearrange to obtain A R A equals z R A minus the identity. Similarly, R B multiplied by B equals z R B minus the identity. These identities do not require A or B to be self-adjoint. Apply the Sylvester operator to K of z. The first term is A R A C R B. The second is R A C R B B. Substitute the resolvent identities. The first becomes z R A C R B minus C R B. The second becomes z R A C R B minus R A C. Subtracting cancels the z-dependent terms. What remains is R A C minus C R B. That is the key cancellation.

slides.title: Integrate around the spectra
slides.lead: Assume first that a single circle contains all of A's spectrum strictly inside and contains no spectral value of B even in its closed disk.
body: Integrate the cancellation identity around that circle and divide by two pi i. The integral of the A resolvent becomes the identity operator, because the circle encloses all of A's spectrum. The integral of the B resolvent becomes zero, because B has no spectrum inside the circle. Hence the integral of R A C minus C R B equals C. Because bounded composition commutes with the operator-valued contour integral, we obtain A times the proposed solution minus the proposed solution times B equals C. Existence is proved.

slides.title: Why uniqueness comes from the same computation
slides.lead: Suppose an arbitrary map X is given and let its Sylvester residual be A X minus X B.
body: Insert that residual into the same two-resolvent integrand. Using the resolvent identities in the opposite direction, one finds that R A times the residual times R B equals R A X minus X R B. Integrate. The first term gives identity times X, and the second gives X times zero. The result is X itself. Thus the contour construction is a left inverse of the Sylvester map as well as a right inverse. It follows that every C has exactly one solution. The Sylvester operator is an isomorphism of Banach spaces, because the contour integral defines a bounded linear map of C.

slides.title: Check the scalar case
slides.lead: Let A multiply by a and B multiply by b, with a different from b.
body: Choose a circle containing a and excluding b. The integrand is C divided by the product of z minus a and z minus b. The integrand has a simple pole at a inside the contour. Its residue is C divided by a minus b. The normalized contour integral therefore gives exactly that value. We have recovered the scalar equation a X minus X b equals C, solved by division by a minus b. The contour formula is the complex-analytic version of that division. For a diagonal matrix, the same residue calculation can be performed in every spectral block.

slides.title: When one circle is not enough
slides.lead: A careful distinction is needed here.
body: Disjoint compact spectra do not always admit one circle that encloses all of A's spectrum while excluding all of B's spectrum. For example, let A have eigenvalues negative two and positive two, and let B have eigenvalue zero. The spectra are disjoint. Any closed disk containing both endpoints contains their midpoint zero, by convexity. So no single circle can contain all of A's spectrum inside its disk while excluding B's spectral value. What do we do? Use a contour made from several positively oriented loops that together enclose A's spectral pieces but avoid B's spectrum.

slides.title: Connection to spectral projections
slides.lead: We met spectral projections earlier by selecting eigenspaces of a self-adjoint matrix.
body: Riesz projections generalize that selection to operators with possibly complex spectra and nontrivial Jordan structure. A Riesz projection associated with a contour is the normalized integral of the resolvent around that contour. It commutes with the original operator and projects onto the spectral component enclosed by the contour. Unlike an orthogonal spectral projection, it need not be self-adjoint for a nonnormal operator. This explains why the Rosenblum proof is so flexible. It needs analytic resolvents and projection identities, not orthogonal eigenvectors or Hilbert geometry.

slides.title: What this lesson establishes
slides.lead: The Sylvester map is invertible for bounded complex Banach-space operators with disjoint spectra.
body: The proof is based on resolvent cancellation, contour spectral projections, and the recovery of any unknown map from its own residual. But there is a separate quantitative problem. How can we prove an explicit estimate for the size of a solution in a useful operator norm? When the spectra have additional separation geometry, an elementary inverse-based argument can give a constant-one bound even on Banach spaces. Before moving on, derive the cancellation identity on paper and evaluate the scalar contour integral. Those two computations are the proof's core.
